• In parallel to developing the Change Impact Analysis approach, initiate informal discussions with line managers or functional heads to gain insight on such matters as existing team structures, role profiles, skillsets, communication and interactions between different teams. This will provide an early view of the organization, prior to conducting the actual change impact analysis, thus helping the practitioner to be more prepared.
  • Practitioners should identify all of the processes to be assessed against the change impact and work with business process owners to collate the current state process documentation so it is readily available for when the practitioner needs to execute the Change Impact Analysis.

Once the importance of executing a Change Impact Analysis has been agreed with the client stakeholder, an approach must be developed to conduct the Change Impact Analysis. The approach should be based on the effectiveness of any previously conducted Change Impact Analysis within the client organization. This opportunity allows for logical thinking through how the Change Impact Analysis should be executed. Depending on the scale of the transformation, the execution of the Change Impact Analysis can involve multiple people and teams across different business units.

The Change Impact Analysis approach should primarily include the process how the client information will be obtained (e.g., independent workshops, surveys, combinations of multiple formats), the level of analysis to conduct (e.g., high-level, detailed, or both), and who should play each of the roles within the change impact analysis workshops.

High Level Change Impact Analyses are conducted against the high-level future operating model or future design, for technology-enabled changes, and are typically conducted at an organization or process-level, not normally detailed to the role or team-level. Detailed Change Impact Analyses are conducted against the detailed future operating model or future design, for technology-enabled changes, and are conducted at a role, team, process and scenario-level. The attendees to include in a typical Change Impact Analysis workshop are line managers or functional heads who understand the daily operations of the respective teams and departments, and can respond to the impacts of any future changes to the people and processes within those teams and departments; business process owners (BPOs) who can provide input on what changes to expect within existing processes; system integrators (for technology-enabled changes) who can provide input on the technology and system specifications that will support the new processes; and the change management team who can facilitate and capture all of the data during the change impact analysis workshops.

It is important to determine how the outputs of the Change Impact Analysis will be turned into intelligent insights and inputs for other program workstreams. Typically, this will include consolidating Change Impact Analysis findings, turning the findings into actions, and communicating and agreeing the actions with a business change governance forum (e.g., Business Readiness Implementation Group (BRIG)). This forum will then cascade the agreed upon next steps to other workstreams (i.e., the BRIG may communicate to the training workstream to roll-out and deliver new training for ‘Department X’ against the identified changes in skills and competencies arising from new processes and systems).

Upon finalizing the approach:

  • Develop a timeline plan for the work that needs to be carried out in order to execute the change impact analysis
  • Consolidate and communicate findings
  • Detail the activities to take place which include aligning owners against each task, completing the timescale and dependencies, and integrating with the overall project plan;
  • Identify the key check-points when the relevant governance forums will be consulted for review during the process.

Upon finalizing the plan, invite relevant business representatives and business process owners to the planned Change Impact Analysis workshops.
